# Heaveball

Heaveball is a spectator-first fictional sports league built around a physical sport for everyday athletes. The playable milestone is an autonomous match that fans can watch, pause and use to understand the sport. The longer-term goal is a league fans can follow between games, with recognizable clubs, persistent players and reporting grounded in what happened on the field.

## Contributor orientation

The current release is a browser-local exhibition between Ember and Harbor. Open the [live Matchroom](https://heaveball-matchroom.hardyburl128.chatgpt.site) to generate squads and watch a match. Reloading starts a fresh session. The public GitHub repository contains the rules, playbook, player-generation spec, history and visual references. Club logos live in `docs/logos/`, named after the team. Each club has the original PNG (for example `southie-dockers.png`), which the league's teams spreadsheet links to by its raw GitHub URL, plus a transparent-background PNG (`-transparent.png`) and a traced SVG for future in-game crests. `docs/logos/make_variants.py` makes the last two from the original. Matchroom’s simulation, renderer and release script live in its separate Sites source repository.

For gameplay changes, edit `src/match.js`. `src/view.js` draws the field and players and handles the handbook and controls. `src/index.html` provides layout and styles. Never edit `dist/`; `tools/build.py` regenerates it. The two textured dirt strips above and below the blue center square identify the no-possession area. Compare rule changes against the current handbook and this summary, especially the four-yard ring and the out-of-bounds ruling when a carried or grounded ball enters a dirt strip. Airborne passes may travel over dirt.

Before releasing, exercise roster generation, the start gate and the affected match rules. For pacing changes, sample full randomized games and report combined scores and possession duration in game-clock seconds. Keep the roadmap below distinct from shipped features. Current playtesting priorities include recognizing off-ball routes, spotting dead balls in the no-possession area and checking that center-zone tackles and runway control affect results.

## Watching a match

The Matchroom uses a dark broadcast design: rounded cards on a near-black ground, Bebas Neue display type with Inter for text, and one mint accent. The pregame screen is a card grid with the matchup and projected spread, team averages, tactics and rules. During play a score card with placeholder club crests sits above the field card, whose control bar holds Pause, the 1×–8× speed control, New match and Full screen. Phones stack the same cards in the same order with the same controls, so desktop and mobile have the same features. A "How to play" button in the header and a Rules button in the field control bar open the rules as an overlay that works before kickoff, during play and in full screen; close it with ✕, Escape or a click outside. The overlay is a visual guide for first-time viewers: a numbered field diagram with a zone legend, point tiles for each way to score, cards for the four pass types, and a what-happens-next list for tackles and restarts.

Ember and Harbor each carry a 12-player roster: eight on the field and four substitutes, two on each of the team's benches. Substitutes appear in the scouting list marked “bench”. The pregame handbook explains the rules and shows both clubs’ average ratings, overall strength and a forecast spread, win probability and projected total. The forecast updates when either club changes tactics. Generate new rosters redraws both teams and updates the comparison before kickoff. Each club draws an offensive playbook and a defensive scheme. Both can be changed in the pregame handbook. Play match starts the selected matchup. The numbered overhead view shows the ball, clock, play-by-play, possession share and runway control. A thin broadcast score bar runs along the top of the field canvas, outside the playing surface, in both the normal and full-screen views. It matches the site's style: a flat dark strip with Bebas Neue type, shield-shaped placeholder crests, both scores in rounded pills (the club with the ball gets a mint outline), possession or the current ruling on the left, and the game clock, period and a mint POSS pill with the current possession length on the right. Narrow screens drop the status text, crests and period. The play-by-play uses broadcast descriptions for meaningful passes, tackles, takeaways, loose balls, penalties and scores. It omits most routine blocks, screens, assignment switches and pass-type labels. The separate Highlights log keeps scoring summaries with game time and running score, plus possession-changing defensive plays in sudden death or in the final five minutes when the score is within five points. Its filter can show scoring plays only. A live box score shows player positions and tracks player and team points, attempts, completions, receptions, Throwing Centers, interceptions, tackles, fumbles, turnovers charged, penalties committed, passes broken up, drops and big hits. The box score also shows team possession averages and a stat legend. Regulation scoring plays hold the field and game clock for five real seconds at all playback speeds. Other stoppages and resets hold for two real seconds so the ruling can be read. A ring or blocking penalty holds the incident for three real seconds before the free-run formation is set. Player scouting connects a jersey to its player, dimensions and skills. Playback opens at 1× and supports pause, 2×, 4× and 8×. The simulation keeps time in a background tab and catches up when browser throttling delays callbacks without skipping broadcast holds. Halftime opens with first-half team totals and an optional stat-leaders page. The 15-second halftime countdown can be frozen or skipped. The final box score opens automatically with team totals and a separate page of individual stats, and can be reopened after dismissal.

The pregame handbook shows both overall ratings and the projected spread above a compact grid of all 12 trait averages. Team tactics and the expandable rules sit alongside the grid on wide screens and below it on narrow screens. The field canvas sizes itself to its on-screen width so the field fills it below the score bar. Full screen resizes the canvas to the whole screen and scales the field to fill it. In landscape the controls stack in a slim column beside the field so most of the screen is gameplay. The field bar has Pause and 1×, 2×, 4× and 8× speed buttons that stay available in full screen and stay in sync with the speed menu below the field. Supported browsers also lock to landscape when entering full screen. Browsers that restrict native fullscreen use an in-page field view. Jersey labels use measured digit bounds for centering. During a contested ground ball, diving players remain upright discs while fallen and shoving players use their respective poses. The dive behavior remains active. Narrow layouts stack the field above scouting and play-by-play. Narrow layouts stack the field above scouting and play-by-play. The build includes the match engine, renderer and dirt texture in the entry page for embedded previews. Each release should update this contributor guide and regenerate and sync both Markdown and Word copies.

## Spread forecast

The pregame spread is a fitted model, not the overall-rating difference. Each club's expected points start from a base of about 29 and add weighted contributions from its own 12 trait averages, the opponent's trait averages, its offensive playbook, the opponent's defensive scheme and its own defense. The spread is the difference in expected points, rounded to the half point. The total is their sum. Win probability treats the final margin as normally distributed around the spread with an 11.2-point standard deviation.

The weights were refitted with ridge regression (penalty chosen by five-fold cross-validation) on 339 headless full matches. These are 300 matches from after the fatigue and defensive-pressure pass, minus their 11 Runway power vs Carrier pressure games, plus 50 new games of that matchup played after the Carrier pressure fix. On held-out matches the model explains about 33% of the variance in final margin. The favorite won about 69% of the time, and the margin's residual standard deviation is 11.8 points, which sets the win-probability spread.

## Strategy balance

Every playbook and defense was tuned against randomized simulations so that none decides a game on its own while each keeps a recognizable style. In the final 1,000-match check, teams scored 26.5 to 32 points a game depending on playbook, and each defense's average scoring margin (its own points minus points allowed) landed within about four points of even.

| Strategy | Signature in simulation |
|---|---|
| Patient passing | Longest possessions, about 55% of the clock, fewest possessions and fewest turnovers |
| Balanced | Even mix of carries, passes and 3-point catches |
| Runway power | Most two-point ring carries, fewest 3-point catches, most turnovers |
| Quick swing | Most passes per possession and the highest completion rate |
| Free flow | Most possessions and the widest mix of scoring plays |
| Ring guard | Fewest ring carries allowed; gives the opponent more possessions |
| Receiver denial | Fewest 3-point catches allowed |
| Star focus | Most passes broken up |
| Passing-lane zone | Lane-reading defenders get extra reach for tips while keeping their ring-side shade |
| Carrier pressure | Most tackles and forced turnovers, with a deep, loose back line that concedes when the press is beaten |
| Runway contain | Funnels runs into tacklers and limits 3-point catches |
| Switch coverage | Steady marks with fewer opponent possessions |

The engine exposes `pressGap` and `rushRead` for Carrier pressure, and `laneStep`, `laneCut` and `laneReach` for Passing-lane zone, so these identities can be adjusted without rewriting the defensive logic.

## Player generation

| Role | Height | Weight | Jersey |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heaver | 5′8″–6′4″ | 170–220 lb | 00–99 |
| Runner | 5′7″–6′4″ | 155–240 lb | Usually 00–40 or 80–89 |
| Anchor | 5′11″–6′5″ | 200–260 lb | Usually 30–99 |

Builds cluster near each role’s midpoint. Jersey numbers are unique within each team. The pool includes #00 and #0, followed by #1 through #99. Runners and Anchors draw from their typical ranges 90% of the time. Ratings span 20–100, with team averages generated across 55–90 OVR. Roughly 85% of matchups explicitly draw an opponent within five overall points, while independent draws allow occasional mismatches. Team quality changes the underlying ratings. The generator preserves role biases toward throwing for Heavers, hands and agility for Runners, and Strength and Tackling for Anchors.

The twelve ratings are Arm Strength, Throw Accuracy, Strength, Speed, Jump, Hands, Reaction, Discipline, IQ, Kicking, Agility and Tackling. The prototype also tracks energy during play. Mass, speed, strength, support and approach angle matter in contact. Roles describe typical strengths and movement eligibility.

## Field and scoring

Two teams play two 20-minute halves on a 50-by-34-yard field. Both attack one four-yard ring in a ten-yard square center zone. Green quadrants permit throwing and running. Yellow runways permit running and handoffs. Every role can traverse the full blue center zone. The central strips belong to neither half. Only Anchors can move beyond them into the opposite half. Off-ball players can cross the dirt, and an airborne pass may travel freely above it. A carrier who enters the dirt on their own concedes a free run lane. If contact drives a carrier into the dirt, or a pass, deflection or loose ball touches the surface, the opponent takes possession at the nearest quadrant. More than three consecutive live game-clock seconds unblocked inside the ring still awards the opponent a free run lane and charges the player a penalty. Leaving the ring, getting blocked or becoming tied up in a pile resets the count.

| Points | Play |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Intercept a pass or recover an opponent's fumble in the center. Keep possession. |
| 2 | Carry the ball from outside the center through the ring. |
| 3 | Catch a teammate’s pass in the center and break the ring line under control. |
| 5 | Catch an airborne save kick in the center before it lands. Either team can score. |

## Venue and sideline

The overhead view shows the area around the field as well as the field itself. All venue measurements are in yards in the `venue` object at the top of `src/match.js`, so the renderer, the engine and any future 3D stadium share one layout. The origin is the field's top-left corner.

- **Surround.** Park fields sit in natural park grass in the same quiet, low-contrast style as the field and the turf: soft color variation, faint sun-dried areas and fine fibers lying in loose directions. All-weather fields sit in synthetic turf: fine fibers laid in 4-yard rolls with faint seams and rubber infill. `tools/generate_surrounds.py` (numpy and Pillow) generates both as seamless tiles in `assets/surrounds/`, each covering 12 yards. The build embeds the park tile in `dist/index.html` beside the default field and copies both to `dist/surrounds/`. The turf tile loads the first time it is needed.
- **Benches.** Four benches sit 4 yards behind the end lines, level with the quadrant centers (y 6 and y 28). Each team has one bench on each half: Harbor's two benches are on the top side and Ember's are on the bottom side. Each bench seats two substitutes.
- **Coach boxes.** There is one white box per team, in diagonally opposite corners beside a team bench: Harbor's is top-left and Ember's is bottom-right.
- **Referee.** One referee, drawn as a black-and-white striped disc, works the dirt strip: the top strip in the first half and the bottom strip in the second half and sudden death. The referee shadows the ball from the middle of the strip. After a reaction delay of 0.22–0.5 seconds, they sidestep any pass predicted to cross the strip below head height within about a yard of them. Their outline turns yellow while dodging. A ball that hits the referee on the dirt is out of bounds with the same ruling as a ball touching the strip: the other team gets a quadrant reset, and the thrower or last player to touch it is charged a turnover. In a 40-match check the referee dodged about 2.3 passes a game and was never hit. With dodging turned off they were hit about 0.37 times a game. Scoring did not change (about 75 combined points a game before and after).

## Substitutions

Substitutions are live and unlimited, and only the team with the ball can make one. Heavers and Runners count as one position for substitutions. They come on from the bench on their own half, because they may never cross halves. Anchors may come on from either bench. Each bench holds one Heaver or Runner and one Anchor, so every Heaver and Runner on the field has a same-half substitute and every Anchor has two.

- **Trigger.** The coach checks for fatigue while the team has the ball and the carrier is set, such as at a quadrant reset or a standing throw. A player is replaced when their energy falls below 50% and an eligible substitute has at least 30 points more energy. The most tired player goes first, and each team makes one substitution at a time.
- **On the field.** The tired player runs until they are past the end line by the bench. Only then does the substitute sprint on from their seat, and the player coming off takes it. The player running off is drawn faded and takes no part in play. The substitute cannot receive the ball until they are inside the lines. The carrier keeps the ball until the substitute reaches their spot, up to six seconds, unless the team is in hurry-up mode. A restart completes any substitution in progress.
- **Recovery.** Bench players recover energy at the resting rate, so a player who came off can return later. Everyone, bench included, is fully rested at halftime.
- **Records.** Players keep their own stats on and off the field. The box score lists all 12 players per team. The play-by-play logs each change, for example “Substitution · Ember #25 Cruz replaces #27 Page (fatigue)”.
- **Sudden death.** No substitutions. Injuries do not exist yet; when they are added, an injury should be able to force a substitution at any time, including in sudden death.

In a 20-match check, teams made about five substitutions a game in total, and scoring did not change.

## Coaches and in-game adjustments

Each club has a head coach with a name and a hidden **adaptability** rating from 25 to 98, clustered around 65. The pregame handbook shows both coaches under their club's tactics. The broadcast does not show the rating. The coach boxes hold the head coaches.

- **Reviews.** Coaches review the stretch since their last change every five minutes of game clock (`reviewEvery`) and at halftime. They need at least four possessions to judge (`coachMinPossessions`).
- **Defense.** If the opponent is scoring more than 1.05 points a possession (`leakyDefense`), the coach may switch schemes at once. The counter comes from `defenseCounter`: Carrier pressure against Patient passing, Switch coverage against Balanced and Quick swing, Runway contain against Runway power, and Balanced against Free flow.
- **Offense.** If their own offense is under 0.6 points a possession (`stalledOffense`), the coach may change playbooks from the team's next restart. The counter comes from `playbookCounter`, chosen against the opponent's defense from the strategy descriptions: Patient passing against Ring guard and Runway contain, Runway power against Receiver denial and Switch coverage, Quick swing against Star focus, Passing-lane zone and Carrier pressure, and Balanced against Balanced.
- **Adaptability.** It sets the chance of noticing: 0.9 × adaptability² at five-minute reviews, so stubborn coaches rarely react mid-half, and 25% + 75% × adaptability at halftime. It also sets the chance of choosing the counter instead of a random scheme (30% + 70% × adaptability). 
- **Overreaction.** Every time the opponent scores, a coach may make a knee-jerk defensive switch without reviewing anything. The chance per score is `OVERREACT_RATE` (0.5915, raised 30% twice from 0.35) × (1 − adaptability)². That allows at most four per half (`overreactPerHalf`, raised from two) and none within one minute of their last change (`overreactCooldown`). The pick is the real counter only 35% of the time; otherwise it is a random different scheme. In a 90-match check, coaches under 55 adaptability overreacted about 1.3 times a game, coaches from 55 to 74 about 0.8, and coaches 75 and up about 0.1. The play-by-play shows it, for example “Ember coach Vance overreacts to the score and switches the defense to Switch coverage”. Average combined scoring stayed within the normal batch-to-batch range (about 64 in this check). The cap of four rarely binds; the chance per score and the one-minute cooldown set the frequency.
- **Effect.** Coaches make about 1.5–2 reviewed changes a game. With adaptive coaches, Runway power against a Carrier pressure start averages about 34 points, down from 38, because coaches move to Runway contain. The play-by-play logs every change, for example “Harbor coach Pryor switches the defense to Runway contain”.

## Hurry-up

Every offense goes to hurry-up in the last 1:30 of the first half (`firstHalfHurry`). Hurry-up means shorter reads and quicker releases, and the carrier does not wait for substitutes. A team trailing by five or more in the last five minutes of the game also hurries, and only then does the opposing defense press. The first-half hurry-up adds about 2 combined points a game. With coaches, the average combined score is about 66 (50-match check), inside the owner's acceptable range of 42–70. The forecast's base was raised by 0.6 per team to match.

## Possessions and restarts

Base player movement and acceleration are 10% faster than the previous build. Standard lob passes travel 10% faster at the same arc height. The existing ball-speed adjustment still applies to passes, kicks and loose balls. Throw distance and Arm Strength determine flight time, while the passer chooses a trajectory for the situation. A **lob** is the standard pass: high-arching, comparatively slow, able to clear defenders and easier to receive. A **line drive** is the quickest, flattest and hardest throw; strong arms use it to hit urgent or quick-swing windows, but its pace makes it substantially harder to catch. A **bounce pass** is slower and easier to handle, and is considered only on a legal same-half path because a bounce on dirt is immediately out of bounds. When teammates are within four yards, they use a gentle underhand toss with a low arc and a longer flight time, including under pressure. At handoff distance they can transfer the ball directly instead. Short hops are exceptionally rare through 16 yards. They become more likely on longer attempts, especially when the passer has lower Arm Strength or Throw Accuracy. Low Accuracy, particularly when Arm Strength exceeds control, can also sail a throw beyond and above the intended receiver. During buildup, carriers can release early when a nearby outlet has separation and the passing lane is clear. Patient possessions, protected leads and designed plays can still call for a longer hold. On drive-and-kick possessions the carrier probes the runway, checks space ahead and fatigue, and retreats to a legal quadrant to pass when the lane closes. Outlet selection considers all roles, including Anchors, using separation, Hands and distance. Players read spacing, run routes on both halves, switch the ball across the field, use short outlets, attack the runway and hand off under pressure. Live carriers search for angles and slow with fatigue. Defenders read the ball, the ring and all eligible opposing receivers, including Anchors. They generally take goal-side positions and update their assignments as the play shifts. Agility and reaction shape jukes. Carriers favor safe throwing angles nearer the blue and can attack an open runway while building possession. When progress stalls or coverage tightens, the offense reads the entry lane and its Anchor matchup again. It can switch to drive-and-kick, a power run, an off-ball block or an Anchor leak before the possession ends. One Anchor can block a receiver’s marker while another draws help on the far side. Anchors remain eligible outlets and handoff options and can join a live pile to add force. Defenders keep a fading estimate of drives and blocks, adjust ring depth and can switch coverage when a block frees a receiver. Routine blocking and coverage exchanges stay visual rather than filling the play-by-play. Quadrant defenders give deep corner outlets more room and shade toward the lane from the ball to the circle. Near-side defenders close from the goal side when a runner commits. Defenders can intercept mid-flight through the crowded middle, bat down an airborne pass or tip it sideways. The chance of a tip or bat is 15% higher on eligible passing-lane reads and contested catches. Height and Jump increase reach, Reaction helps a defender respond in time, and Speed helps close the remaining distance to the ball. Passes can also rebound off a receiver or skip past their hands. The simulation tracks ball height, velocity and spin. The ball is a softball-sized rubber ball on turf, so grass, runway turf and dirt produce visible skips but low restitution and rapid vertical energy loss rather than superball rebounds. Directional player impacts can still redirect it. The view renders a plain white ball and a ground shadow that shifts and softens with height. A carrier near the ring can move the ball to the hand that gives it a better path across the line. The displayed ball position determines whether it has entered the ring. The ball stays live unless it lands or rolls out or another rule stops play. Throw Accuracy, trajectory and coverage shape completions. Height, Jump, Reaction and Hands give players a small edge on contested catches, and deflections stay live until they touch an out-of-bounds surface. Wide-open catchable balls are dropped about 0.2–1.5% of the time. Most drops come from contested or crowded catch points. Hands and Throw Accuracy moderately affect drops in traffic. On short approaches, carriers are more likely to attack the circle when their available blockers can account for the defenders ahead. Broadcast calls describe the action without naming every pass type; three-point passing scores still show throw distance. A pass caught inside the ring for a three-point score earns the passer a Throwing Center. Routine reads slightly favor Heavers and Runners as outlets while Anchors remain eligible to catch, carry and score.

A quadrant tackle produces a stationary throw from the tackle spot. A runway tackle turns the ball over. A dive stopped short also turns it over, while a center catch stopped short retains possession. Incompletions stay live. Loose-ball pursuit is selective rather than team-wide. Each club sends its quickest realistic arrival based on proximity, Speed, Reaction and IQ, may add a second player only when already close enough to affect the contest, and caps the battle at four pursuers. Players without a viable path hold their coverage, outlet or ring position. An uncontested pickup can still be clean and immediate. In traffic, nearby players dive, fall, push and shove while the ball stays at ground level and moves only a short distance between bodies. Proximity, Hands and Reaction shape pickups, with Strength carrying extra weight on contested fumbles. Form tackles use the Tackling rating alongside strength, momentum, size and support. Isolated stops are harder against an even matchup. Missed jukes and defender size advantages make clean tackles easier. A fast, heavier carrier can drive through a smaller defender. A defender also has a small chance to rip the ball directly from a carrier. The strip matchup combines Strength, Hands, Reaction and IQ for both players and releases a live loose ball. Big hits favor size, closing speed and a direct approach. Matches can finish with zero to 20 combined big hits. Six to twelve is the usual target, with occasional quiet and more physical matchups. They can shake a carried ball loose or knock a pass away at the catch, sending the ball bouncing into live play. A recovered fumble still restarts in the nearest quadrant. Near a boundary, a defender with inside leverage can push a carrier out of bounds for a turnover at the nearest quadrant. It can also happen in a pile, at lower odds. An off-ball player who is pushed out can return in bounds. Evenly matched piles rock back and forth. A pile ends in a stop after 4.5 game-clock seconds without gaining 0.65 yards toward the ring or when the carrier is driven 1.25 yards back from their closest point. The same thresholds apply on free run lanes. Weight and height contribute moderately while Strength supplies most of the driving force. Nearby support adds directional force, so a much stronger team ordinarily moves a weaker group steadily toward the ring. Tackling and IQ build a defender’s chance to finish the stop. The carrier’s Strength, Hands, IQ and Agility help maintain control or pull out for a quadrant reset. Pile pressure can cause a fumble. A rare free teammate can receive a concealed handoff, and a desperate pass out of the pile usually becomes a wild live ball. The box score charges turnovers for lost fumbles, interceptions thrown, runway tackles that give up possession and out-of-bounds turnovers. Penalties have their own count. A free run lane gives the offense a Runner and blocker against two defending Anchors. A tackle there retains possession. A scoring club chooses the next restart quadrant after scoring two, three or five and must vary consecutive choices.

Quadrant-center resets pause for 1.5 simulation seconds. Defenders align goal-side of their marks, Anchors spread along the runway seams, and runway Runners begin two yards from the backline on offense or five yards from the center boundary on defense.

## Play calls and sudden death

- **Airborne rescue.** An errant throw keeps its normal flight time. A teammate chases it only if their position, momentum, Speed, Agility and Reaction give them a chance to reach the sideline. The player must be outside the line and within kicking reach of the descending ball. Most errant throws go out. A successful kick starts at the ball’s contact position and height. Kicking skill, reach and body momentum affect the return. Most returns are short, and a clean strike can reach the blue for a rare five-point catch by either team. An uncaught in-bounds return stays live.
- **Quick swing.** The carrier holds the ball briefly and reads the ring before choosing another outlet. A clear lane can bring a quick pass into the blue or a run through the runway. The ball can work between two or three quadrants, go all the way around, or keep moving for up to eight outlet passes (two full trips around the four quadrants). Teams can reverse direction or skip across the field either way between Q2 and Q4 or Q1 and Q3 when the passing lane opens. If the outlets close or the sequence reaches eight exchanges, the team returns to its usual reads. Every playbook can use this tempo when the spacing suits it. It is most common for Quick swing and rare for Runway power.
- **Corner boomerang.** Five percent of quadrant setups call for a deep same-half outlet and a return pass to the original passer cutting into the blue. The offense can switch back to its usual reads if either leg closes.
- **Anchor leak.** An Anchor shows a lead block, then releases into the blue as a receiver. Balanced and Free Flow carry the call, and the offense can also switch to it mid-possession.
- **Last-step handoff.** Balanced, Runway Power and Free Flow can call a runway attack with a trailing carrier. The exchange comes as the first carrier draws a nearby defender.
- **Three-on-three runway.** A regulation tie goes to sudden death. A coin flip sets first possession, and each side fields three Anchors, a Runner and a Heaver. The offense sends its three Anchors against the three defensive Anchors. Turnovers start the new carrier at the back of their runway. The first score ends the match.
- **One-point ambush.** Defensive coaches decide when to show an opening at the edge of the blue and send one Anchor to jump it. Coaches favor the call when chasing a late deficit and hold it back when protecting a late lead.
- **Restart choices.** Scoring teams favor a quadrant with weaker opposing passing or a favorable defensive matchup and alternate choices. This is part of routine restart strategy.

## Offensive playbooks

Each playbook and defense has a short broadcast-style `blurb` shown under its menu in the pregame tactics card (for example, Runway power: "Downhill runs behind big Anchor blocks"). The full pros and cons below stay in each strategy's `description` and appear as a tooltip on the blurb.

| Playbook | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Patient passing | Protects the ball, sustains possession and makes the defense survive repeated reads. Safer throws and deliberate holds reward disciplined passers. | Creates fewer scoring chances, can stall against carrier pressure and may consume too much clock while trailing. |
| Balanced | Can answer most coverages by mixing swings, drives, blocks, leaks and handoffs. It has the fewest built-in matchup liabilities. | Does not impose one dominant pressure point. Results rely on the carrier recognizing the right answer and executing it. |
| Runway power | Creates direct ring opportunities, uses size and blocking, and punishes a light or isolated front. | Produces shorter, more physical possessions with extra tackle and fumble exposure. Runway contain and talented tacklers are difficult matchups. |
| Quick swing | Most often uses short holds and quick passes among open quadrants to set up a ring attack by pass or run. | Every exchange creates another catch or deflection opportunity. Switch coverage can follow the sequence, and bounce passes cannot be used to change halves. |
| Free flow | Lets athletes attack the space they see, stays unpredictable and changes calls when a defense overplays the first action. | Its shared reads are demanding. Misread spacing, aggressive throws and improvised decisions make outcomes more volatile. |

The engine applies these identities to release time, passing risk, run appetite and mid-possession choices. They remain situational rather than automatic: ratings, spacing, score, clock and the opposing scheme still decide the play.

## Defensive schemes

| Scheme | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Balanced | Keeps two goal-side helpers, matches dangerous eligible receivers and has no glaring structural weakness. | Does not fully erase an elite runner, a star receiver or rapid ball movement. |
| Ring guard | Puts three defenders near the ring, sharply reduces clean ring entries and creates defensive scoring chances through tackles, tips and interceptions. It is strongest with athletic players and talented tacklers. | Concedes deep outlets. Its defense-first posture also produces shorter offensive possessions and fewer clean offensive chances, so much of its scoring must come from defensive plays. Opponents must patiently move and dissect it. |
| Receiver denial | Gives eligible receivers tight goal-side marks, lowers easy completions and makes the carrier hold or run. | Leaves only one dedicated ring helper. Blocks, handoffs and individual athletic mismatches can break the coverage. |
| Star focus | Denies the best Runner and Heaver, then brackets the more dangerous star near the ball. | Secondary receivers and the far side receive more room. Quick reversals force the help to travel and can punish the extra attention. |
| Passing-lane zone | Crowds anticipated throwing lanes and raises the likelihood of interceptions, tips and batted passes. | Short outlets, patient overloads and quick swings can find seams between zones. It also gives receivers space to settle outside the lane. |
| Carrier pressure | Sends an extra defender to shorten the carrier’s read, hurry throws and create immediate turnovers. | A clean outlet, handoff or broken first tackle gets behind the pressure and leaves less help at the ring. |
| Runway contain | Spreads three helpers across run lanes, funnels direct attacks toward tacklers and is the best structural answer to Runway power. | Gives up deeper quadrant outlets and can be stretched by disciplined passing or legal center relays. |
| Switch coverage | Exchanges assignments quickly against cuts, blocks and swing sequences, preventing one screen from freeing a receiver. | Generates fewer aggressive takeaways and can lose physical isolations. A late or low-IQ switch can still expose the ring. |

The play-by-play identifies each club's scheme and the players targeted by Star focus. Each entry aligns its timestamp with a single message column, keeping team-colored player names inline as the text wraps. On a free run lane, the lead Anchor screens the help defender so the Runner can isolate the first tackler. The play starts when the penalty popup clears. Both defenders can adjust their positions before contact. A tired Runner keeps at least 82% of their movement speed on the approach. The tackler can grab and slow the Runner until help arrives, or lunge for a difficult stop at the spot. A Runner can slip a grab, break free before help arrives, or stay up through a missed lunge. Sudden death uses its own formation. All active players can still use the full center zone in sudden death.

## Fatigue and defensive pressure

This pass brought average combined scoring down from about 70–75 to about 62 (300-match check). It made fatigue matter and gave defenders more ways to disrupt passes. All the constants named below sit near the top of `src/match.js`.

- **Fatigue.** Players tire whenever they move faster than 40% of top speed (previously 48%). The base drain is `FATIGUE_RATE`. The hidden stamina rating scales it through `STAMINA_SPREAD`: a stamina-40 player drains about twice the base rate and a stamina-95 player about a quarter of it. Tired players lose up to 15% of their speed off the ball and 26% with it (previously 10% and 20%). Their drop risk on contested catches doubles. This produces about 10–11 fatigue substitutions a game. Players subbed off average about 61 stamina against a roster average of about 70.
- **Tips in traffic.** Every extra body within three yards of the ball beyond the first two raises the tip and bat chance by `TRAFFIC_DEFLECT` (300%), both in flight and at the catch. Tips and bats roughly doubled, from about 7 to about 13 a game. Completion fell from about 89% to about 87%.
- **Defensive gambles.** A defender whose IQ, Reaction and Speed average 68 or more sometimes jumps a pass of 12+ yards. Only tight coverage qualifies: the defender must be within 4.5 yards of the intended receiver and 1.5–9 yards from where the ball will be just before the catch. They must also be able to reach its height, stay on a half they may legally enter, and get there in time. The landing point must be in bounds and catchable. Like a safety reading the passer's eyes, the defender breaks before the release: they get 0.15–0.4 seconds of read time, scaling with their ratings, and run at full speed plus 10% with no ramp-up. Passers with low IQ and Discipline telegraph their throws. They draw up to twice as many gambles and give longer reads, while sharp passers draw as few as half. `GAMBLE_RATE` sets the base rate, which gives about one attempt a game. The success roll is 30% to 50%, scaling with the defender's ratings. Counting defenders who arrive a step late, about 30% of resolved gambles succeed. A success is an interception (more likely with good Hands) or a knockdown. A miss, or failing to get there, leaves the defender stumbling at 30% speed for 1.6 seconds, unable to contest catches or deflections.
- **Smothered passers.** When a defender who is both taller and faster than the passer is within 1.8 yards, the throw's scatter widens (up to 60% more with `SMOTHER_ERROR`). An errant throw becomes more likely (up to +4 points with `SMOTHER_WIDE`). On a lob or line drive the defender may tip it at release (up to 20% with `SMOTHER_TIP`). The effect scales with the height and speed edge and how tight the defender is. Player generation is unchanged; this applies only when such a matchup happens, about 0.1–0.2 release tips a game.
- **Throwing out of a crowd.** Each defender within 2.5 yards of the passer beyond the first adds `RELEASE_TRAFFIC` (8 points) to the chance of a tip at release on lobs and line drives, capped at 35%.
- **Fumble scrambles.** Contested fumble recoveries can bobble up to six times instead of three. Each recovery is `FUMBLE_SCRAMBLE` (14 points) more likely to squirt loose again, and each bobble lasts a little longer.

**Carrier pressure against run-first offenses.** Carrier pressure plays a loose back line, keeping marks 2.8 yards goal-side of receivers. Against Runway power that let the offense throw into an open center for 3 points, about 65 points a game in that matchup. Against a `groundFirst` playbook, Carrier pressure now tightens its marks to `pressRunCushion` (1.6 yards). It also keeps one defender home `homeGuardDepth` (3.2 yards) in front of the ring. The matchup now averages about 41 points for Runway power in 50 games. Tighter marks did most of the work; the home defender alone changed little.

**Strategy balance after this pass (300 matches, adjusted for the fix).** Points per team by playbook: Patient passing 29.0, Balanced 31.7, Runway power about 34 (about 33 against every defense except Carrier pressure, about 41 against it), Quick swing 27.3, Free flow 31.1. Every defense's average margin is within about four points of even. Runway power is still slightly the strongest playbook. A planned coach-adaptability rating, letting coaches change tactics during a game, may cover the rest. Otherwise it can be made more stubborn about drive-and-kick throws. The strategy table below predates this pass.

## Gameplay targets

Regulation game totals can range from 0 to 100 combined points. The owner's acceptable range for the average combined score is 42–70. The current build averages about 66 (see Hurry-up; it was about 62 before coaches and the first-half hurry-up). IQ and Discipline influence a carrier’s estimate of runway space, a passer’s ability to recognize defenders in the passing lane, and a help defender’s choice to switch or stay with a dangerous cutter. Defensive Anchors shade closer to the ring, contact matters on contested receptions and defenders have a modest advantage finishing a tackle. The scoring values still come directly from the play. Possession length depends on opportunity, offensive playbook and defensive identity. Each new team draws a playbook with a baseline aggression and a set of preferred opening calls. Runway power reads the runway before committing. Anchor screens open gaps, misdirection handoffs change the runner, and passes can lead a Runner into space or reset the ground attack. A closed lane sends the carrier back to look for an outlet. Patient passing, Balanced, Free flow and Runway power teams take progressively earlier chances on average, while Quick swing releases the ball fastest. Teams ordinarily circulate through a few safe exchanges before committing to a set play. A near-side outlet helps a covered carrier move the ball before contact. A far-side airborne pass may cross above the dirt, but a bounce pass never changes halves and any ball touching dirt is immediately out of bounds. When the runway closes early, a carrier can circle back into a legal quadrant and throw while play continues. Players favor shorter and clearer lanes during buildup, with an exception for a well-supported run. Each call still affects how quickly the passer reads an outlet and how readily a carrier takes an open lane. Mid-possession adjustments can change that appetite for risk. In the last five minutes, a team trailing by five or more attacks sooner and sends a defender to press the ball. In the last two minutes, a team leading by five or more favors short outlets and uses more clock. Long possessions can still develop when a patient team keeps finding outlets. These targets guide randomized match testing. Fans should be able to see how an open outlet, a strong block or a timely stop changed a possession.

## League and media roadmap

The current browser prototype generates fresh exhibition matches. The planned league layer would retain player and club identities, schedule games and record standings, statistics and season history. Shared broadcasts would reveal events as they air. Once clubs have logos, the home club's logo will be spray-painted into the center zone beneath the ring and blended into the grass: drawn over the field texture and under the field lines, partly transparent and multiplied into the grass so the texture shows through, with slightly rough edges like real field paint. Recordings of player and ball movement alongside the event log would support replays, highlights and box scores. Pregame stories, recaps and ongoing media coverage would use those same records so a fan could trace a headline to the play that earned it. Persistent seasons, synchronized broadcasts, replay archives and an automated newsroom are future work.

## Source and release workflow

The sport repository holds the revised rulebook, coaching playbook, player-generation specification and fictional history. The Matchroom Site uses a browser simulation, a canvas renderer and a pregame interface. The simulation includes runway-only sudden death. Substitutions remain on the roadmap; the 12-player rosters and benches are in place for them. A 3D stadium is a later goal and is not being built yet; for now the venue is planned and drawn in the overhead view. [Sport repository](https://github.com/miniappmike/heaveball)

Maintain the project scope in this file as features change. Running `python3 tools/build.py` rebuilds `dist/` from `src/` and `assets/`: it inlines the game into `dist/index.html`, embeds the default field texture, copies the other textures and writes `dist/summary.md` with a build record. The build needs only Python 3.

Field templates provide high-resolution park surfaces with clay no-possession zones and all-weather synthetic turf in several colorways. Select a field above the match and the choice is remembered in the browser.

The footer uses accessible GitHub and OpenAI logo links to the production Matchroom on GitHub Pages and the GPT test site for Codex Matchroom PR builds.

## Mobile fullscreen

The field fills the mobile viewport with black margins and overlaid playback controls. The match page stays vertically scrollable in native fullscreen and in the viewport fallback.

## Player markers

A small on-field stamina bar appears under the carrier and any other player below 35% stamina. Green means 70% or higher, yellow means 35% to below 70%, and red means below 35%. Each player has a hidden stamina rating. Heavier players tend to rate a little lower, with individual conditioning varying within each weight class. Sustained running and contact drain stamina. Slower movement and rest recover it, and halftime restores it. Below 55%, fatigue gradually reduces acceleration and speed, with a larger speed effect for ball carriers. Very tired players are slightly more likely to drop a pass in traffic. The free run lane floor still applies before a grab.

Players keep their numbered circles during loose-ball scrambles. Nearby players pursue if they can reach the ball. The others reposition to cover space or offer an outlet for the recovery.

## Calls and stoppages

Scores, penalties, turnovers and ordinary stoppages freeze play in place for 3.5 seconds. A tackle that keeps possession pauses for 2 seconds with no popup, and the tackled player wears a black inner ring until the next possession. Big plays show a large popup in the middle of the field: CENTER! (blue) for 2-, 3- and 5-point scores, TAKEAWAY! (orange) for 1-point center-zone interceptions and fumble recoveries, TURNOVER (red), PENALTY (yellow, with the penalized player in red) and OUT OF BOUNDS (white) when the same team keeps the ball. A loose ball that touches the dirt shows BALL OUT OF BOUNDS. When a pile drives a carrier into the dirt, the badge shows NO POSSESSION ZONE and the opponent restarts in the nearest quadrant. Both show the awarded team and whether it gains or retains possession. Badge subtitles identify the player as Team #number Name, with the name in team color. Pausing holds the popup on screen.

## Penalties

Every penalty awards a free run lane: three seconds unblocked in the ring, a block in the back, a Runner or Heaver crossing past their own half, and a carrier entering the no-possession zone on their own. Contact that drives the carrier into the dirt awards a quadrant reset. Low IQ and Discipline make penalties more likely. Typical rates per match: about 0.7 half crossings, 1–2 no-possession calls, 2–3 ring-time calls and 2–4 blocks in the back.

Sport documents and reference images live in `docs/`. Matchroom source is split into `src/` (hand-edited), `assets/` (textures), `tools/` (build and texture generator) and `dist/` (generated).
